## Three notes, and every one of them has a job

Sound C, E and G together, then take one away and listen to what leaves with it.
Drop the E and the chord stops telling you whether it's major or minor. Drop the
G and the remaining pair loses the frame that was holding it steady. Three notes
carry a lot of information, and each one carries a different part of it.

A *triad* is a root plus two notes stacked a third apart. Count those thirds in
semitones for now: a major third spans four, a minor third spans three. Stack 4
then 3 and you get major. Stack 3 then 4 and you get minor. Two 3s give
diminished, two 4s give augmented. Writing each quality as a two-element array
lets one constructor build all four, which puts the audible difference right
next to the number that caused it.

## Four qualities from two numbers each

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84
use_synth :piano

define :make_triad do |root, thirds|
  [root, root + thirds[0], root + thirds[0] + thirds[1]]
end

define :play_both_ways do |notes|
  play_chord notes, release: 1.2
  sleep 2
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.45
    sleep 0.5
  end
  sleep 1
end

qualities = {
  major: [4, 3],
  minor: [3, 4],
  diminished: [3, 3],
  augmented: [4, 4]
}

qualities.each do |name, thirds|
  triad = make_triad(note(:c4), thirds)
  puts "#{name}: #{triad}"
  play_both_ways triad
end

puts "matches Sonic Pi: #{make_triad(60, [4, 3]) == chord(:c4, :major).to_a}"
```

Every root here is C, so major and minor differ at exactly one pitch. Listen to
the middle note first. Before you press Run, which of the four do you expect to
sound the least settled? Each chord arrives twice: once as a block, where the
tones fuse into a single object, and once as an arpeggio, where you can walk up
the two stacked intervals one at a time.

## Move the root, then reverse the stack

1. Change the root from `:c4` to `:a3`. Every pitch takes the same offset, so
   the chord moves house and changes name without changing quality. Follow the
   spacing and you'll hear the same four characters in a new register.

2. Reverse `[4, 3]` to `[3, 4]` and compare the two directly. The lower third
   shrinks, the upper third grows, and major turns into minor while the outer
   frame stays at seven semitones. One swap, one changed note.

3. Switch to `:prophet` and lengthen the release. Neighbouring arpeggio notes
   now overlap and start to fuse into the block chord, though the attacks still
   show you the order in which the stack was built.

## The outer interval matters as much as the inner one

The root is a reference address. The first third is an offset from that address,
and the second is an offset from the middle note. Cumulative addition turns two
local distances into three playable pitches. You already did this arithmetic to
build a scale; here it's the same operation with three notes and bigger steps.

Quality changes the frame, not only the filling. Major and minor both span a
perfect fifth, seven semitones from root to top, which is why they can trade
places in a progression without disturbing much around them. Diminished pulls
that frame in to the six-semitone tritone from [Lesson 19](../04-intervals/19-interval-sound-dictionary.qmd). Augmented pushes it
out to eight. So the altered third changes the chord's stability, and stability
is a stronger effect than colour.

Here's what the semitone arrays throw away. A written triad is a stack of
letter-name thirds, and two spellings that share piano keys don't have to share
a harmonic meaning. This constructor works at the sounding-pitch layer on
purpose. When a chord enters a key or a printed score, keep its spelled root and
quality beside the generated integers so that later notation code never has to
guess how a pitch got its role.

The final `puts` compares your constructor against Sonic Pi's built-in
`chord(:c4, :major)`. Passing that check proves the arithmetic agrees. It says
nothing about whether the synth and release you picked make the four qualities
easy to tell apart, which is a question only your ears can answer.

## A drill that changes one variable

Build yourself a ten-trial listening drill from the four entries in `qualities`.
Start with `use_random_seed 42`, pick a quality and a root somewhere between MIDI
48 and 59, play the arpeggio and then the block, leave four beats for your
answer, then print the name.

Hold synth, rhythm, amplitude and register span identical across every trial.
That consistency strips out the clues that have nothing to do with interval
structure, so a tally of your confusions becomes real evidence about what you
can and can't hear yet. Keep the tally. [Lesson 27](27-inversions-voicing.qmd) keeps these same three pitch
classes and moves them into different registers, and you'll want to know how
securely you recognise the plain version first.
